text:
A lithium-ion cell is charged with a two-stage protocol called constant-current, constant-voltage (CC-CV), and in the first stage the charger forces a fixed current into the cell, typically between 0.5C and 1C, where 1C is the current that would fill the nominal capacity in one hour. The cell voltage rises steadily during this stage, because the voltage is set by the cell's state of charge and by the extra voltage needed to push current through its internal resistance. When the terminal voltage reaches a ceiling, usually 4.1 to 4.2 V for common chemistries, the charger switches to the second stage, where it holds the voltage fixed and lets the current decay on its own. Charging ends when the current falls to a small threshold, often 0.05C to 0.1C.

Charging slows near full because of what the voltage limit means physically: lithium ions are shuttled from the cathode into the graphite anode, and the cell's open-circuit voltage rises as the anode fills with lithium. The terminal voltage you measure is the open-circuit voltage plus the current multiplied by the internal resistance, along with additional polarization losses from slow ion transport and charge-transfer reactions at the electrode surfaces. Early in charging, the open-circuit voltage is well below the limit, so a large current fits within the voltage budget. As the cell fills, the open-circuit voltage climbs toward the ceiling, and the headroom left for the resistive and polarization terms shrinks. To keep the terminal voltage at the limit the current must fall, and the decay is roughly exponential, like a capacitor charging through a resistor, though the analogy is imperfect.

The limit exists because pushing the voltage higher accelerates damage, driving electrolyte oxidation at the cathode and potentially causing metallic lithium to plate on the graphite, which permanently loses capacity and creates safety risks. Diffusion also matters, since lithium must diffuse into the particles of active material, and as the surface fills, the concentration gradient driving ions inward flattens, so the interior fills slowly. This slow solid-state diffusion is part of why the cell needs a long tail at low current to reach a truly uniform full state.

The practical result is that the CC stage delivers roughly 70 to 80 percent of the capacity in well under an hour, while the CV stage may take as long again to deliver the rest. Fast-charging systems exploit this by stopping early, accepting 80 percent, because the last stretch is slow and the time is better spent elsewhere. Temperature also plays a role, since cold cells have higher resistance and a greater plating risk, so chargers reduce current or warm the cell. Battery management systems monitor voltage, current, and temperature for each cell to enforce these limits, and they balance cells in a series string so that none exceeds its ceiling.
